name: Regulatory Change Mapping
title: Regulatory Change Mapping
answer: Regulatory change mapping is the practice of tracking new statutes, rules, guidance and court decisions that affect how an organisation may use artificial intelligence, then connecting each change to the internal policies, contracts and controls it touches. In practice it sits between the legal team and the compliance function, and it covers both binding instruments and softer material such as regulator guidance and enforcement notices. The output is usually a structured register that records what changed, when it takes effect, which business units are affected and what action is required. It is distinct from general horizon scanning because the mapping step ties each change to a specific obligation or document inside the organisation.

sections.body: Regulatory change mapping is the practice of tracking new statutes, rules, guidance and court decisions that affect how an organisation may use artificial intelligence, then connecting each change to the internal policies, contracts and controls it touches. sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a mix of official sources and commercial tracking services. Primary material comes from legislature websites, regulator publications, court dockets and official journals, while secondary services aggregate and tag that material for faster review. Internally, teams typically use a document management system, a spreadsheet or a dedicated compliance platform, and increasingly a large language model to summarise long texts and suggest which internal policy is affected. This site maintains 229 compliance and regulation pages and tracks 7166 state AI bills, which illustrates the volume any mapping process has to absorb. The infrastructure question is less about storage than about keeping identifiers stable so that a change can be traced from source text through to the internal control it modifies.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical cycle starts with monitoring, where analysts watch defined sources for new items and screen them for relevance against a taxonomy of topics such as transparency, data protection, employment and sector rules. Relevant items are then read in full, summarised, and mapped to the obligations and internal documents they affect, often with a risk rating and an owner assigned. Reviewers confirm the mapping, and the register is published to the teams that need it, with a change log so that later readers can see what moved and why. Because the volume is high, many teams triage first and deep-read only what passes a materiality threshold, which makes the taxonomy and the threshold itself recurring points of debate.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Provenance matters here because a mapping is only as good as the source it cites, so each entry should record the issuing body, the publication date, the version and a link to the original text. Where a summary is produced by a model, teams increasingly keep the prompt, the model version and the raw output alongside the human-reviewed version, so that a later reader can tell what a machine wrote and what a person changed. Access control and retention rules apply to the register itself, since it often contains privileged analysis and commercially sensitive planning. On intellectual property questions in particular, the site tracks 150 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, and 29 AI case law precedents, which shows why litigation status is usually recorded as a separate field from enacted law. Nothing in a mapping register is legal advice, and readers should treat it as a pointer to the primary source rather than a substitute for it.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward faster cycles and more granular mapping, as legislatures and regulators issue AI-specific instruments at a pace that manual review struggles to match. Expect more emphasis on machine-readable publication by regulators, on stable identifiers that let tools link a rule to a control automatically, and on audit trails that distinguish machine summarisation from human judgement. Cross-border mapping will stay difficult because the same technical practice can be permitted in one jurisdiction and restricted in another, so teams will likely maintain parallel registers rather than one global view. The practical test for any mapping function will remain whether it helps a reader find the current, correct source quickly and understand what, if anything, their organisation needs to do about it.
